problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{3{n}^{3}(2{n}^{2}+1)}{(4{n}^{3}-5)(4{n}^{3}+5)}$ for $n\ge 1?$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of a Factored Rational Sequence
examples.problem: What is the limit of the sequence $a_n = \dfrac {n(3n-7)} {(3n-1)(3n+1)}$ for $n\geq 1?$
examples.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
a_n=\dfrac {n(3n-7)} {(3n-1)(3n+1)}=\dfrac {3 n ^ 2 - 7 n} {9 n ^ 2-1}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim_{n \to \infty}  \dfrac {3 n ^ 2 - 7 n} {9 n ^ 2-1}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $n^2,$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by $n^2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{3{n}^{2}-7n}{9{n}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{3{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{7n}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{9{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(3-\frac{7}{n})}{(9-\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{3-0}{9-0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is $\dfrac 1 3.$

feedback.problem:
Which of the following sequences diverge?

- ${a}_{n}=\frac{n-1}{{n}^{3}+1}$ for $n\ge 1$
- ${a}_{n}=\frac{2}{{n}^{3}}$ for $n\ge 1$
- ${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}+3}{3{n}^{2}-n}$ for $n\ge 1$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each sequence in turn. We need to calculate the limit of each sequence as $n$ approaches at infinity.

- In sequence I, the dominant term in the denominator is ${n}^{3},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n-1}{{n}^{3}+1} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }⁡\frac{(\frac{n}{{n}^{3}}-\frac{1}{{n}^{3}})}{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }⁡\frac{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{n}^{3}})}{(1+\frac{1}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{0-0}{1+0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence II, the limit is

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{3}}=0.
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence III, the dominant term in the denominator is $3{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{3}+3}{3{n}^{2}-n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{3}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{3{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{n}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(n+\frac{3}{{n}^{2}})}{(3-\frac{1}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n+0}{3-0} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

In conclusion, sequence III diverges.
